newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian rebels kill 28 in village night massacre.
newsitem.headline: Algerian rebels kill 28 in village night massacre.

text.p: Moslem fundamentalists killed 28 people in an isolated Algerian village in the early hours of Sunday. Hours later a bomb ripped apart a cafe in an Algiers suburb wounding 53 people, hospital sources and witnesses said.
In the latest slaughter in the vast North African country, security forces said the 28 people were killed in the village of Dhamnia in Ain Defla province, some 120 km (75 miles) southwest of Algiers.

The overnight raid was the fifth mass killing this month in which the authorities say a total of 82 people have died, many with their throats slit. It followed a month marked by even more bloodshed, termed by one paper "The Month of all Horrors".
The security force statement on the official Algerian news agency APS said the 28 villagers were killed by a "group of terrorists", Algeria's term for Moslem fundamentalists.
They gave no other details.

News of the killing coincided with that of a bomb attack early on Sunday in the Algerian capital where hospital sources and witnesses said 53 people had been wounded. The official toll by the security forces was 20 wounded.
Algeria's unelected quasi-parliament, in a bid to tighten control of weapons, on Sunday passed a law on "materials of war, arms and ammunition".

It gives the Defence Ministry control of the "manufacture, import and export of weapons of war", which range from military weapons to knives. Anyone usurping that function faces life jail. It tightens the categories of those who may carry arms. Second-time offenders on weapons, including hunting rifles, can face the death penalty.
The use of knives to kill civilians has become common, spreading even deeper horror among Algerians.

"Such atrocities have created an atmosphere of terror, where people fear not just being killed, but being killed in these particularly brutal ways," said Amnesty International in its November 1996 report on Algeria.
"If I must be killed, I pray it is by bullet and not by having my throat cut," the London-based human rights group quoted a university lecturer as saying.
Thousands of people have fled villages in fear to take refuge in towns and cities since their communities became targets of mass killings in darkness in November.
Early that month 31 people were slaughtered in Sidi El Kebir near the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers. All had their throats cut and many were mutilated.
"I'm leaving Sidi El Kebir for anywhere, provided there is more mercy there," said one boy as villagers prepared to bury their friends and relatives.
Three nights earlier, 10 women and three children were killed in a similar night of bloodshed, which Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour called "ignoble savagery".
Shortly afterwards, Algerian papers reported hundreds of people leaving scattered communities, with some sleeping in the streets of Blida, headquarters of the No. One military region.
The killings continued.
Ten people died on an isolated farm near Blida on December 5. A further 19 were found dead the following day in a nearby village.
Twenty more were killed in mid-December, dragged from a bus stopped at a fake roadblock in Blida province.
On December 24, Algerian security forces said "a group of terrorists" had killed six civilians overnight in Algiers.
Bombings too continued, refocusing violence on overcrowded Algiers and defying the authorities' claims to have wiped out most of those responsible, leaving only "residual terrorism".
A bomb exploded on Sunday inside a cafe in the working class suburb of el Harrach, in the southern edge of Algiers, wounding 53 people, hospital sources said.
It was the fourth blast within one week in which 18 people were reported to have been killed and 210 wounded in Algiers.

About 60,000 people have been killed since violence erupted in the North African country after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the Moslem fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken an overwhelming first-round lead.
